body:
Formation of the Mughal painting tradition

The Mughal School of Miniature Painting developed in northern India from the 16th century. It combined Persian artistic conventions with existing Indian painting traditions. Over time, Mughal painters also incorporated selected European visual elements.

The Mughal court supported an organised atelier, or workshop, in which painters, calligraphers, gilders and bookbinders worked on illustrated manuscripts and albums. Paintings recorded royal activities, historical events, portraits, hunting scenes, religious and literary narratives, and the natural world.

Mughal painting is especially associated with careful observation, detailed portraits and increasingly convincing representations of people, animals and landscapes. However, these features developed gradually; the early Mughal style was more strongly influenced by Persian models.

Humayun and the Persian connection

Humayun came into close contact with Persian miniature painting during his exile at the court of the Safavid ruler Shah Tahmasp. He subsequently invited the Persian master painters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad, also written Abd us Samad, to work for his court.

Humayun established a painting workshop known as the Nigaar Khana, connected with his royal library. His patronage provided an important foundation for the large-scale artistic activity that followed under Akbar.

Akbar and the expansion of the imperial atelier

Akbar (1556-1605) employed both Persian and Indian artists. Their collaboration helped produce a distinctive Mughal style that was more varied and dynamic than a simple reproduction of Persian painting.

Akbar's commissions included illustrated histories, narrative literature and Persian translations of Indian texts. Paintings frequently show several figures engaged in action, with carefully distinguished costumes, buildings and landscapes.

Major illustrated works

WorkNature of the workAssociation
HamzanamaIllustrated adventures of HamzaBegun under Humayun; continued on a large scale under Akbar
RazmnamaPersian translation and illustration of the MahabharataCommissioned by Akbar; illustrated project completed in 1589
AkbarnamaHistorical chronicle of Akbar's reignAssociated with Akbar's court and Abu'l Fazl
RamayanaIllustrated episodes from the Indian epicTranslation and illustration undertaken under Akbar

The Hamzanama: an important exception

The Hamzanama is one of the most ambitious early Mughal painting projects. Its illustrations were produced on comparatively large cloth-based folios, with narrative text on the reverse. They supported the oral narration of stories.

The project is traditionally described as comprising 14 volumes and about 1,400 illustrations, produced over approximately 15 years, with the main work dated around 1567-1582. Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad supervised its production.

The Hamzanama demonstrates that an illustrated manuscript associated with the miniature tradition need not always consist of physically tiny pictures.

Important artists under Akbar

Daswanth, also written Daswant, was associated with the illustrated Razmnama. Basawan was an important painter of the Akbari atelier, noted for expressive figures and increasingly naturalistic treatment. Miskin was another distinguished painter, associated with subjects ranging from historical and literary narratives to animals.

Early Mughal paintings were often collaborative works. Therefore, naming a master artist associated with a manuscript does not necessarily mean that the master personally painted every illustrated folio.

Prelims focus

  • Humayun: Invited Persian painters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad.
  • Akbar: Developed a major imperial painting atelier with Persian and Indian artists.
  • Hamzanama: Adventures of Hamza; the main illustrated project dates approximately to 1567-1582.
  • Razmnama: Persian Mahabharata, associated with Akbar's translation and illustration programme.
  • Akbarnama: Historical account of Akbar's reign.
  • Trap: The Razmnama is not a Persian translation of the Ramayana.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part II, Class 12, reprint 2026-27, Chapter 3, The Mughal School of Miniature Painting, pp. 35-42; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Chapter 9, Painting, pp. 100-101.]

body:
Jahangir: Portraits and close observation of nature

Jahangir (1605-1627) inherited an established imperial painting workshop but developed his own preferences. Where many of Akbar's greatest projects were extensive illustrated narratives, Jahangir placed increasing emphasis on individual portraits, naturalistic studies and carefully finished paintings.

Artists paid close attention to the distinguishing features of birds, animals and plants. Court paintings also attempted to represent the recognisable appearance of rulers, nobles and other individuals.

Jahangir's interest in painting is reflected in his memoirs, known as the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri or Jahangirnama. Paintings could be preserved individually in richly decorated albums called muraqqas, rather than forming part of a continuous narrative manuscript.

Ustad Mansur and natural-history painting

Ustad Mansur was a prominent painter associated with Jahangir's court. He specialised in the careful depiction of birds and animals. Jahangir honoured him with the title Nadir ul Asr, meaning Wonder of the Age.

Important examples include his painting of a falcon perched on a bird rest and a zebra presented at Jahangir's court in 1621. Such paintings are valuable examples of the Mughal interest in representing the distinctive appearance of real animals.

Abul Hasan and symbolic royal imagery

Abul Hasan was another celebrated artist at Jahangir's court. His work Jahangir's Dream, dated approximately 1618-1622, represents a politically symbolic meeting between Jahangir and the Safavid ruler Shah Abbas.

Although Mughal painters often produced recognisable portraits, this painting is not a straightforward record of an actual meeting. It uses symbolic imagery to convey the emperor's desired image of power.

Bichitr was also associated with the imperial atelier. His work Jahangir Enthroned on an Hourglass, dated around 1625, is a well-known example of symbolic Mughal court painting.

Jahangir-period painting combined two different interests: accurate observation of nature and symbolic representations of imperial authority. Naturalism does not mean that every painting depicted an event exactly as it occurred.

Shah Jahan: Formality and imperial splendour

Under Shah Jahan (1628-1658), Mughal painting continued to develop, but the dominant courtly taste became increasingly formal, refined and idealised.

Royal portraits emphasised dignity, magnificent clothing, jewels and carefully arranged ceremonial settings. Detailed representations of courts, processions and imperial occasions strengthened the visual image of the emperor's authority.

The Padshahnama, a richly illustrated chronicle of Shah Jahan's reign, is a particularly important example of this phase. Its paintings represent the grandeur of the imperial court through elaborate composition and finely rendered detail.

Later Mughal painting and the regional courts

During Aurangzeb's reign, the imperial painting workshop received less emphasis than it had under some earlier rulers. Nevertheless, painting at the Mughal court did not cease immediately.

As imperial patronage changed and regional courts expanded, artists and paintings circulated more widely. Mughal conventions influenced several regional schools, including those of Rajasthan, the Himalayan hills and the Deccan. These regional traditions did not simply copy Mughal painting; they combined its features with their own earlier styles and local subjects.

Prelims focus

  • Jahangir: Detailed portraits and naturalistic studies of birds, animals and plants.
  • Ustad Mansur: Celebrated animal and bird painter; title Nadir ul Asr.
  • Abul Hasan: Associated with Jahangir's Dream.
  • Bichitr: Associated with Jahangir Enthroned on an Hourglass.
  • Shah Jahan: Formal imperial portraits and the illustrated Padshahnama.
  • Trap: Aurangzeb's reign did not bring an immediate and complete end to Mughal painting.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part II, Class 12, reprint 2026-27, Chapter 3, The Mughal School of Miniature Painting, pp. 42-54.]

body:
The Rajasthani painting tradition

Rajasthani miniature painting developed in several princely states of Rajasthan, particularly from the 16th to the early 19th century. Important centres included Mewar, Bundi, Kota, Bikaner, Kishangarh, Jodhpur and Jaipur.

These courts were associated with Rajput ruling families, which explains the older term Rajput painting. However, that term was once applied broadly to paintings of Rajasthan, central India and the Himalayan hills. Modern study usually distinguishes the Rajasthani and Pahari schools, while recognising their historical connections.

The Rajasthani schools shared an interest in literary and devotional themes, but each court developed its own preferred subjects, colours, landscapes and figure types. Mughal influence was particularly strong at some centres, while others retained a bold indigenous appearance.

Important literary and devotional themes

The Ramayana and Bhagavata Purana supplied religious narratives, while poetry associated with Radha and Krishna inspired paintings of love, devotion and changing emotional states.

Several named literary works are especially important for identifying the subject of a painting:

  • Gita Govinda: A Sanskrit poem by Jayadeva, composed in the 12th century, associated with the love and devotion of Radha and Krishna.
  • Rasamanjari: A work by Bhanudatta dealing with types of lovers and their emotional states. Artists often interpreted its themes through Radha and Krishna, although the original text does not itself name Krishna.
  • Rasikapriya: A work by Keshav Das, composed in 1591, describing states of love and relationships, frequently represented through Radha and Krishna.
  • Ragamala: A series of pictorial interpretations of musical ragas and raginis, representing moods through human or symbolic scenes.
  • Baramasa: Paintings expressing the seasons and emotional associations of the 12 months of the year.
  • Bihari Satsai: A celebrated collection of verses by Bihari Lal, illustrated by painters at several courts.

Rajasthani painters also represented royal hunts, processions, festivals, battles and portraits. Thus, the tradition was not limited to religious themes.

Major regional schools

SchoolImportant patron or artistIdentifying featureWork or subject
MewarJagat Singh I; SahibdinBold narrative scenes and prominent reds and yellowsRagamala; Bhagavata Purana; Ramayana
BundiBhoj Singh; Rao Chhattar Sal; Bhao SinghLush vegetation, dramatic hills and romantic landscapesChunar Ragamala; Baramasa
KotaRam Singh I and later Kota rulersEnergetic animal studies and hunting scenesRoyal hunts and animal chases
BikanerAnup Singh; RuknuddinRefined Mughal influence and relatively subdued coloursRasikapriya; Ramayana
KishangarhSawant Singh; Nihal ChandElongated faces, curved eyes and lyrical landscapesBani Thani; Radha-Krishna paintings
Jodhpur or MarwarMarwar Rajput rulersBold regional subjects alongside Mughal-influenced portraitsDhola-Maru; royal portraits
Jaipur or AmerSawai Jai Singh II and Jaipur rulersStrong Mughal court influence and polished portraitureCourt portraits and literary illustrations
MalwaRegional patrons of central IndiaFlat compositions and strongly marked colour areasRagamala paintings

Mewar: Sahibdin and the illustrated epics

Mewar was an important early centre of Rajasthani painting. An illustrated Ragamala series was produced at Chawand in 1605 by the artist Nisardin.

Painting flourished under Jagat Singh I (1628-1652). The painter Sahibdin produced a Ragamala series in 1628, illustrations for the Bhagavata Purana in 1648, and the Yuddha Kanda of the Ramayana in 1652. Another artist, Manohar, illustrated the Bala Kanda of the Ramayana in 1649.

Mewar paintings are useful examples of how painters converted extended narratives into images. Their compositions often use prominent colour areas and distinct arrangements of figures to make a complicated story readable.

Bundi and Kota: Related courts, different strengths

Bundi developed a vigorous tradition known for its treatment of vegetation, hills, water and romantic settings. The Chunar Ragamala of 1591 is associated with its early phase under Bhoj Singh.

Kota emerged from the same political and artistic setting; the two were separated in 1625. Kota painters became especially celebrated for royal hunting scenes and lively depictions of animals in forests.

Both schools might contain dense landscapes. The particularly strong emphasis on the excitement of the chase is an important identifying clue for Kota.

Bikaner and Jaipur: The Mughal connection

Bikaner maintained close links with the Mughal court. During the reign of Anup Singh (1669-1698), manuscripts and paintings were collected and preserved. The artist Ruknuddin combined indigenous, Mughal and Deccani features, while the earlier artist Ustad Ali Raza had worked under Karan Singh.

Jaipur also developed under strong Mughal influence. Its painting tradition originated at Amer. Sawai Jai Singh II established Jaipur as the new capital in 1727 and supported painters and the royal painting establishment known as the Suratkhana.

Kishangarh: Sawant Singh, Nihal Chand and Bani Thani

Kishangarh is distinguished by highly stylised facial features, especially large curved eyes, long arched eyebrows, a slender pointed nose and an elongated face.

The important patron was Sawant Singh, who wrote devotional poetry under the name Nagari Das. The painter Nihal Chand worked for him and developed the characteristic Kishangarh treatment of Radha and Krishna.

The painting Bani Thani, associated with Nihal Chand, is a celebrated example. Bani Thani was a singer and poet who became associated with Sawant Singh. In the paintings, her idealised appearance was connected with the representation of Radha.

Prelims focus

  • Mewar: Sahibdin; Ragamala and illustrated Ramayana.
  • Bundi: Lush landscapes; Chunar Ragamala of 1591.
  • Kota: Particularly associated with hunting scenes.
  • Bikaner: Anup Singh and Ruknuddin; strong Mughal influence.
  • Kishangarh: Sawant Singh, Nihal Chand and Bani Thani.
  • Trap: Bani Thani is associated with Kishangarh, not Kangra.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part II, Class 12, reprint 2026-27, Chapter 2, The Rajasthani Schools of Painting, pp. 10-34; NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, Chapter 9, The Making of Regional Cultures, pp. 128-129, 2020-21 edition.]
